Maladaptive Strategies.value: I think about how life would have been different if the event had not occurred
Open or exposed spaces where I feel vulnerable
constantly scan environment for signs of threat

Threat.value: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
I always identify escape routes before I feel comfortable anywhere

Memory.value: There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Negative Appraisals.value: I should have protected others and I failed
The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am
My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe

issues.item: Triggers: Pregnancy/Birth Reminders: Pregnancy, childbirth, or babies in general
issues.explanation: For a 45-year-old female auditor with combat trauma, 'Pregnancy/Birth Reminders' is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items and downstream threat items center on hypervigilance, pursuit, and danger cues, whereas this item implies a reproductive/perinatal trigger theme that is not supported by the memory, threat, appraisal, or strategy content. It looks disconnected from the combat-based formulation rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Restrict Eating: control eating strictly to feel in control
issues.explanation: 'Restrict Eating' is weakly integrated with the rest of the profile. The dominant clinical pattern across triggers, threat, memory, and appraisals is fear-based hypervigilance and fragmented trauma memory, with maladaptive strategies of avoidance and rumination fitting that pattern. Restrictive eating instead suggests a separate control/body-management coping style that is not reflected elsewhere in the selected items, making it clinically hard to explain as part of the same combat-related PTSD profile.

vignette: Lina, a 45-year-old auditor of Lebanese descent, returned home from Afghanistan after a harrowing night in which a sudden explosion shattered the quiet of a forward operating base. She now wakes to dream residue, the vivid taste of burnt earth and the echo of gunfire; the scent of a familiar perfume in the city's subway or the thud of a distant construction blast can instantly set her heart racing. Each of these triggers pushes her into a maze of counterfactual thoughts-she should have taken a different route, she could have protected more-and forces her to scan the air around her, as if a shadow lurks in every corner. Her recollection is a mosaic of gaps and fragments. She can remember the heat of the mortar shell and the smell of gasoline, yet the sequence of events-who was where, who survived-slips away like sand. This incomplete picture keeps gnawing at her, and she blames herself, convinced that her own character made the tragedy possible. The memory of the night, fractured and partial, fuels the feeling that danger is always present; the belief that she failed to protect others amplifies the threat that now clings to her every thought. Her sense of self-flawedness turns ordinary scents and sounds into triggers that keep her in a constant state of vigilance. The constant sense of threat forces Lina to remain in narrow safe zones-her apartment, a locked office corner, a parking garage with a single exit. Before she can breathe, she maps escape routes in her mind, avoiding any open spaces where she feels vulnerable. That underlying threat makes ordinary scents and sounds feel potentially dangerous, turning a faint perfume or a sudden bang into a trigger that snaps her into high alert. While she checks behind every door, the memory of that night keeps resurfacing, each fragment tightening her self-critical voice, which in turn amplifies her perception of danger. The ever-present sense of threat reinforces her belief that she has failed, deepening her self-critical voice. At the audit firm, the open-plan layout feels like a battlefield to Lina. The bright fluorescents and the free flow of glass walls make her check behind each colleague's desk, and the faint scent of a client's perfume in the break room sends a rush of panic through her. She counters by standing near the server room, where the hum of machinery masks any external noise, and she rehearses escape routes through the stairwell, always ready to flee if a sudden sound erupts. Each time she scans, the act of monitoring her surroundings heightens her sense of threat, reinforcing the belief that she can never trust her own body. The memory of the combat night pieces together as she checks, each fragment tightening the web of guilt that spirals her thoughts. This cycle of avoidance has eroded Lina's confidence at work. When a supervisor asks her to present audit findings in an open meeting, she postpones, fearing the bright lights will trigger a nightmare. She has missed deadlines, and colleagues remark that she "seems distracted." The counterfactual thoughts-if she had been present, the project could have succeeded-flood her mind, making her feel she has failed again. Her sense of threat and self-critical voice only grow louder as she isolates herself from the team. Unable to endure the constant fear and the professional decline, Lina finally decided to seek help. She is most afraid that confronting her memories will shatter her fragile sense of safety, yet she hopes therapy can untangle the web of triggers, thoughts, and avoidance that has held her back from living a full, productive life.
